description: Kam Labs is a Nigerian hardware + AI startup (NVIDIA Inception). We build computer-vision systems for football clubs and field-capture tools for farms and forest reserves. Skills: Python, CV/ML, geospatial data, web apps, hardware. For Field Shift we'll build a farm planner for Nigerian smallholders from NASA POWER, SMAP and IMERG, checked against our own ground footage. Looking for: remote sensing/GIS, agronomy or climate science, and UI/UX design. Real farms, real data, real deployment.
summary: Field Shift is a crop-rotation planner for Nigerian farms built on NASA Earth observations. Pick a farm, or click any point in Nigeria, and it reads 35 years of daily satellite weather for that spot. It answers three questions in plain language. Has my rainy season changed? When is my field bare and exposed? Which rotation fits the season I have now? It grows 16 rotations, from maize every year to cereal–legume, intercrop, double-crop and cover-crop systems, through every real season from 2009 to 2025. It then compares the farmer's current rotation with the three best fits for their priorities: reliable harvest, income, soil health, water and livestock feed. Each recommendation shows why it was suggested, the evidence from the data, the soil benefits, the risks to check locally, and what the data can't tell us. In Kano, the rains now start three weeks later and the season is 17 days shorter. Field Shift shows that, and recommends a sorghum + cowpea → groundnut rotation that adds ~51 kg N/ha a year and breaks the Striga cycle.
details:
What it does. Field Shift is a decision-support web app for smallholder farmers and the extension officers who advise them. For any point in Nigeria it shows:

1. How the season has shifted. Start of rains, end of season, length of the growing period, seasonal rain, false starts, longest dry spell and days ≥ 35 °C, for 1991–2008 vs 2009–2025, plus a bar for every season since 1991.

2. When the field is bare. Monthly rain vs evapotranspiration and NASA root-zone soil wetness, with each rotation's crops laid over the year. Bare-field months and erosive storms on unprotected soil are visible at a glance.

3. Which rotation fits. 16 rotations are grown in the model through every recent season. The farmer's current rotation is compared with the three best fits for their stated priorities. Each card lists why, evidence, soil benefits, risks to check locally and data gaps.

4. What if. Sliders cut or raise rainfall by up to 30% and add up to +3 °C, re-running every season.

Farmers set their own soil type (sandy/loam/clay), slope, field elevation and priorities. The app says throughout that it supports, and does not replace, local expertise.

How it works. Start of rains uses the Sivakumar (1988) agronomic definition: 20 mm in 3 days, not followed by a 7-day dry spell. A trigger that is followed by one counts as a false start. End of season comes from a daily soil water balance: rain in, FAO-56 Hargreaves reference evapotranspiration out, with bucket size set by soil type. Each crop in each rotation is sown at the confirmed onset of every season. It is checked for season length, usable rain vs need, dry spells and heat at flowering (and cool temperatures for potato), and the reasons for any failure are kept. Rotations are scored on reliability, relative income, nitrogen balance, residue, erosive storms on bare soil (scaled by slope), Striga risk, plant-family breaks, water use and forage. Scores are weighted by the farmer's priorities and normalised across the options for that farm. Everything is deterministic: every sentence in a recommendation traces back to a number.

What we found while building it. NASA POWER's rainfall (PRECTOTCORR) isn't usable for season work in Nigeria. It contains impossible days (1,173 mm in one day at Mista-Ali, Plateau, in 2020), years inflated 3–6× (6,144 mm in 2021) and collapsed years (Kano 2023: 310 mm). We compared it with GPM IMERG and CHIRPS through NASA SERVIR's ClimateSERV. We kept CHIRPS, which is anchored to rain gauges and matches Kano's ~900 mm normal, and kept NASA POWER for temperature and soil wetness. The app shows the comparison for each farm. We also found that POWER's ~55 km grid sits ~300 m below Jos Plateau farms. Correcting temperature to the NASA SRTM field elevation moved Irish potato at Bokkos from 59% to 94% of seasons, which matches where Nigeria actually grows it.

Results across nine demo farms. The Sudan and Sahel savanna (Kano, Sokoto, Maiduguri) and Zaria get sorghum or millet intercropped with cowpea, followed by groundnut. The Guinea savanna and forest edge (Abuja, Mista-Ali, Makurdi, Ibadan) get maize followed by cowpea in the same season. In Makurdi's yam belt, false starts have risen from 6% to 24% of years.

Benefits. A farmer or extension officer gets a season calendar and rotation options grounded in that farm's own 35-year record, in plain language, with honest limits. The approach is open and repeatable for any point in Nigeria, with no login and no API keys.

What we hope to achieve. We want to pilot with extension services and farmer cooperatives on the Jos Plateau and in Kano. We plan to add Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo (with voice), to validate the rain record against farmer rain gauges and Kam Labs' field-capture footage, and to add SMAP and NDVI checks of bare-field periods.

Tools. JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), Leaflet, Chart.js, Node.js (data pulls and tests), Python (deploy, media), ffmpeg. Static site hosted on kamhq.com. Source code: https://kamhq.com/fieldshift/field-shift-source.zip
